content: Community-based settings for PEP distribution can include pharmacies, community organizations, drop-in centers, mobile clinics, and online platforms. Expanding PEP availability to locations closer to where people live and work, with fewer barriers, can significantly improve access. The World Health Organization (WHO) and its Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed evidence on community-based PEP distribution. A systematic review identified six studies evaluating PEP in community settings, including one effectiveness study, three case studies, one study on values and preferences, and one cost analysis. The effectiveness study, known as the SEARCH SAPPHIRE study, was conducted in rural Kenya and Uganda. PEP uptake was highest in community settings (46%) compared to outpatient departments (9%) and antenatal care settings (3%). Over 24 weeks, PEP selection remained highest in community settings (23% at week 24), while uptake in outpatient and antenatal settings was significantly lower. No studies reported on the quality of PEP services, timeliness of uptake, linkage to additional services, or adverse events. However, feasibility studies demonstrated that PEP delivery in community settings, such as out-of-facility sites, police stations, and online platforms, is practical. For example, in Kenya and Uganda, health workers trained to deliver PEP in community settings achieved high completion rates with no serious adverse events. Similarly, in Zambia, police were trained to provide PEP to sexual assault survivors, though uptake was limited by operational hours. WHO has existing recommendations for community-based delivery of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and PrEP, which have been successfully implemented in several countries. A survey of sexual and gender minorities in New York City found interest in receiving PEP and other HIV prevention services in collective sex venues, though privacy concerns and stigma were noted as potential barriers. Cost analyses suggest that community-based PEP is cost-effective in most scenarios, with long-term savings due to reduced ART needs and clinic visits. The GDG concluded that community-based PEP delivery offers clear benefits, including earlier and increased access, reduced stigma, and improved equity in HIV prevention. Task-sharing, where responsibilities are redistributed among healthcare teams (e.g., nurses, pharmacists, community health workers), was strongly recommended to enhance PEP availability. Training, supervision, and equitable remuneration for providers are essential, along with stigma-free and non-judgmental service delivery. Evidence from task-sharing studies supports its feasibility and acceptability. For instance, in Kenya, private pharmacies successfully delivered PEP, and in the UK, nurse prescribers became key providers of PEP. Surveys of healthcare workers in Canada and other countries showed strong support for non-specialist-led PEP delivery. Clients also expressed preferences for nurse-led services due to improved accessibility, anonymity, and quality of counseling. Despite very low certainty of evidence, the GDG issued a strong recommendation for community-based PEP delivery, citing its feasibility, acceptability, cost-effectiveness, and potential to reduce HIV-related inequities. Research gaps include optimizing PEP timing and duration, operational studies on delivery models, and cost-effectiveness analyses in diverse settings.
